title: Self-Regularization with Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable LLM-based Classification

problem.claim: LLM embeddings can contain unintended sensitive or task-irrelevant features that cannot be manually removed, creating challenges for regulatory compliance and classifier generalizability.

gap.claim: LLM embeddings are opaque and difficult to interpret, limiting control over unintended latent features.

contributions.claim: A framework identifies and regularizes unintended features in LLM latent spaces.
A sparse autoencoder is pre-trained and then fine-tuned on task-specific datasets to extract interpretable, task-relevant features.
A classifier regularizer minimizes similarity between classifier weights and identified unintended features.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe the framework as novel and characterize the work as pioneering controllable text classification on LLM latent spaces.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The framework was evaluated on toxic chat detection, reward modeling, and disease diagnosis.
The authors report improved classifier generalizability when features not semantically correlated to the task are regularized.
The authors report that code and data are publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLM contextual embeddings provide automatic and effective representations for text classification.
These embeddings obscure unintended features that may affect compliance and generalizability.
The framework extracts interpretable features with a sparse autoencoder and regularizes unintended features during classifier training.
The framework is evaluated across three real-world tasks and is reported to improve generalizability.
The authors position the work as enabling controllable classification while addressing generalizability, fairness, and privacy challenges.

source_observation.claim: Interpretable latent features can be used to target task-irrelevant behavior during classifier training.

interpretation.claim: Separating feature identification from task-specific regularization may provide a practical control mechanism for opaque representation spaces.

application.claim: This pattern may apply to classification settings where sensitive or task-irrelevant representation features need to be reduced.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which unintended features can be reliably identified or how performance changes across specific conditions.

unknowns: No quantitative results, metrics, baselines, or statistical comparisons are provided.
The abstract does not specify the datasets, model configurations, or regularization settings.
The abstract does not detail fairness or privacy measurements.
The abstract does not provide implementation or reproducibility details beyond the reported code and data availability.
